Sheridan|United States of America.f: Sheridan was the proposed capital of Absaroka, a secessionist state movement that never succeeded, from 1935 to 1939.

Scottsbluff|United States of America.f: Scottsbluff briefly held Nebraska's cold record at minus 46 F in February 1899, until Bridgeport logged minus 47 a week later.

Cody|United States of America.f: Founded in 1896 and named for Buffalo Bill, Cody calls itself the Rodeo Capital of the World.

Latrobe|United States of America.f: The banana split was invented in Latrobe in 1904 by pharmacist David Evans Strickler.

Akron|United States of America.f: Akron was America's fastest growing city in the 1910s, with its population rising 201.8 percent in ten years.

Riverton|United States of America.f: Riverton got its name because four rivers meet there.

Ogden|United States of America.f: Ogden is the closest sizable city to Promontory Summit, where the first transcontinental railroad was joined in 1869.

Champaign|United States of America.f: The first Farm Aid concert was held in Champaign in 1985, drawing 80,000 people and raising over $7 million for farmers.

Eau Claire|United States of America.f: Eau Claire means clear water in French, and legend says explorers on the muddy Chippewa River cried out at the clearer Eau Claire River.

San Angelo|United States of America.f: San Angelo began as Santa Angela, named for the founder's wife Carolina Angela, until the Postal Service insisted on San Angelo in 1883.

Evansville|United States of America.f: Evansville built 6,242 P-47 fighters in World War II, almost half of all the P-47s made in the United States.

Wilmington (NC)|United States of America.f: Workers at the North Carolina Shipbuilding Company in Wilmington built 243 ships in the five years it operated during World War II.

Marion|United States of America.f: Marion, Illinois, is named for Revolutionary War general Francis Marion, known as the Swamp Fox.

Eugene|United States of America.f: Eugene was first called Skinner's Mudhole before it became Eugene City in 1853, named for settler Eugene Franklin Skinner.

Aspen|United States of America.f: Aspen, first called Ute City, surpassed Leadville as the most productive US silver-mining district in 1891 and 1892.

Santa Maria|United States of America.f: Santa Maria took its name in 1885 because mail meant for it kept being sent by mistake to Central City, Colorado.

Appleton|United States of America.f: Appleton's Vulcan Street Plant, which began running on September 30, 1882, was the nation's first hydroelectric central station.

Columbus (MS)|United States of America.f: In 1866 women in Columbus decorated Union and Confederate graves alike, inspiring the poem The Blue and the Grey.

Newport News|United States of America.f: Newport News built Hilton Village in World War I, the first government-built planned community, with 473 English-village-style homes.

Valdosta|United States of America.f: Valdosta is named for Governor George Troup's plantation, which he named after the Aosta Valley in Italy.

Asheville|United States of America.f: Asheville's Biltmore House is the largest privately owned house in the United States, with 178,926 square feet of floor space.

Saginaw|United States of America.f: Saginaw factories made more than half a million M1 carbine rifles for the US military during World War II.

Augusta (GA)|United States of America.f: During the Civil War, Augusta was home to the vast Confederate Powderworks.

Brunswick|United States of America.f: Brunswick's shipyard completed the SS William F. Jerman in just 34 days in late 1944.

Elmira|United States of America.f: Elmira's Civil War prison held 12,123 Confederate soldiers, of whom 2,963 died, and prisoners nicknamed it Hellmira.

Greenville (MS)|United States of America.f: After Union troops burned every building at the original site during the siege of Vicksburg, Greenville was rebuilt three miles away.

North Platte|United States of America.f: The North Platte Canteen, run by volunteers from 1941, served nearly seven million servicemen during World War II.

St Augustine|United States of America.f: Founded in 1565, St. Augustine is the oldest continuously inhabited European-established settlement in the contiguous United States.

Springfield (IL)|United States of Americ.f: Springfield was originally called Calhoun, after Senator John C. Calhoun, until the town renamed itself in 1832.

Bloomington|United States of America.f: State Farm was founded in Bloomington in June 1922 by retired farmer George J. Mecherle as a mutual auto insurer for farmers.

Fort Smith|United States of America.f: Judge Isaac Parker, the Hanging Judge, sentenced 160 people to death at Fort Smith, and 79 were executed.

Lake Havasu City|United States of Americ.f: Lake Havasu City's founder bought London Bridge for $2.5 million in 1968 and had it reassembled there by 1971.

Hobbs|United States of America.f: Hobbs swelled past 12,000 people in the oil boom after the 1927 discovery, then shrank to about 3,000 in the Depression.

Lafayette|United States of America.f: Lafayette was founded in 1821 as Vermilionville and was renamed for General Lafayette in 1884.

Owensboro|United States of America.f: Owensboro hosted the last public hanging in the United States, on August 14, 1936.

Springfield (MO)|United States of Americ.f: Springfield's Five Star Jubilee was the first network color TV series to originate outside New York City or Hollywood.

Tallahassee|United States of America.f: Tallahassee was the only Confederate state capital east of the Mississippi River not captured by Union forces.

Kingsport|United States of America.f: Kingsport, designed as a garden city in 1917, built some of the earliest traffic circles in the United States.

Kenai|United States of America.f: A 97 lb 4 oz king salmon caught in the Kenai River in 1985 set a world record for the largest sport-caught Chinook.

Carlsbad (NM)|United States of America.f: Carlsbad is named after the famous Karlsbad spa in Bohemia, now Karlovy Vary in the Czech Republic.
